summary: Orgyen Jikdral Chöying Dorjé studied under Jamgön Kongtrül Lodrö Thaye and Jamgon Ju Mipham Gyatso. He also taught Shechen Gyaltsab.
Orgyen Tendzin Norbu studied under Patrul Rinpoche and Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo. He later taught Khenpo Shenga.

Specializing in Tibetology and Buddhist studies, Almogi studied at Ngagyur Nyingma Institute, under Khenpo Wangchuk Sonam in 1995, and under David P. Jackson and Lambert Schmithausen. She held posts at the Nepal-German Manuscript Preservation Project and the University of Hamburg (attested 2004–2007).

Hayashima worked in Buddhist studies, philosophy, and Indology, studying under Noritoshi Aramaki and at the University of Hamburg (1992). He held posts at Nagasaki University (attested 1979–1984, 1995–2003), Shiga University of Medical Science (attested 2003–2013), and Ryukoku University (attested 2013–2015).
Working in Buddhist studies and Japanology, Osamu Izumoji held academic posts at Kyoto Prefectural University and Ryukoku University.

Oba was a scholar of Sinology and history and archaeology. He studied at Kansai University (~1948–1953) and held posts there (~1958–1998), at Kogakkan University (~1998–2002), and at the University of the Sacred Heart.

Specializing in Buddhist studies and history and archaeology, Takata studied under Baiei Henmi. He held positions at Tohoku University (attested 1961) and served as head of fine arts at the Tokyo National Research Institute for Cultural Properties (attested 1967).

A linguist, Bergin studied at University College Cork (~1891–1895), the School of Irish Learning (~1903–1904) under Kuno Meyer, and the University of Freiburg (~1904–1906) under Heinrich Zimmer. He held posts at University College Dublin (~1909–1940) and DIAS (~1940–1941).

Hinüber works in Indology, Buddhist studies, and linguistics. Educated at Tübingen, Erlangen-Nürnberg, and Mainz under Paul Thieme, he served at Mainz (1965–1981), directed the Nepal Research Centre, and held the Chair in Indic Studies at the University of Freiburg (1981–2006).

Bopearachchi studied at the University of Kelaniya (~1974–1978), CNRS (1983), Panthéon-Sorbonne University (Ph.D. 1987), and Paris-Sorbonne University (Habilitation 1998). He became Emeritus Director at CNRS in 1989 and Adjunct Professor at UC Berkeley around 2014.

Sirén worked in Sinology and history and archaeology, earning his doctorate at the University of Helsinki (1897–1900). He held posts at Stockholm University (1908–1923), Harvard and Yale (1916–1917), the Musée Guimet (1924–1925), and the Nationalmuseum (1926–1945).

Frank studied at the University of Paris (~1814–1817) and in London (~1817–1818). He held professorships at the University of Bamberg (~1804–1807), the University of Würzburg (1821), and the University of Munich (1826), having previously taught at Banz Abbey School and Kaiser-Heinrich-Gymnasium Bamberg.
An Indologist, Tanaka studied under Naoshiro Tsuji at the University of Tokyo (~1925–1928). He later served as a professor at Chuo University (~1957–1974).
Blau studied at the University of Halle (1848), the Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg under August Friedrich Pott (~1848–1850), and the University of Leipzig (~1850–1852).

Fischer worked in Sinology, Japanology, and history/archaeology. After studying at Tübingen, Munich, Vienna, and Göttingen, he served as director of the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart (1920) and Kunstmuseum Basel (1927), and was an associate professor at the University of Basel (~1927–1937).

Franke worked in Sinology, Indology, and Buddhist studies. After studying at Freiburg, Göttingen, and under Wilhelm Grube, he held chairs in East Asian studies at the Hamburg Colonial Institute/University of Hamburg (1910–1923) and the University of Berlin (1923–1931).

Höfler was a scholar in linguistics and history and archaeology. Educated at Vienna, Lund, and Kiel, he held posts at Uppsala (1928–1934), Kiel University (1935), the University of Munich (1938–1945, 1954), and the University of Vienna (1957–1971).

A scholar in history, archaeology, and linguistics, Jahn studied at Kiel, Leipzig, and Berlin. He subsequently held academic positions at Kiel University (~1839–1847), the University of Greifswald (~1842–1847), the University of Leipzig (~1847–1851), and the University of Bonn (~1855–1869).

A scholar in Sinology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and archaeology, Maenchen-Helfen studied at Vienna, Gothenburg, and Leipzig under August Conrady. He held posts at the Marx-Engels-Lenin Institute (1927–1929), Mills College (1939–1947), and UC Berkeley (1947–1962).

Neugebauer studied at Graz, Munich, and Göttingen, where he also taught (1923, 1928–1933). He held professorships at the University of Copenhagen (1933–1939) and Brown University (1939, 1947–1969), and was later a permanent member at the Institute for Advanced Study (1980–1990).
